analysis.one_liner: Bans all neurotoxic organophosphate pesticides from food.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on: introduced with 5 cosponsors and referred to committee, it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make any food containing an organophosphate pesticide illegal to sell. Organophosphates are nerve-agent-related insecticides; the EPA already banned the most notorious one, chlorpyrifos, from food in 2022, but other organophosphates could still legally leave residues on food. This bill would shut that door for the whole class, regardless of any pesticide-tolerance levels the EPA had set.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially pregnant women and young children, since organophosphate exposure is linked to neurological harm; the bill would remove the entire class of residues from food rather than regulate them level by level.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers, especially children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new section to the food-safety law declaring any food that bears or contains an organophosphate pesticide, or a residue or breakdown product of one, to be unsafe, and it applies regardless of any tolerance the EPA had allowed.
The EPA banned chlorpyrifos, one organophosphate, from food in February 2022, but the bill would cover the entire organophosphate class, closing the gap left by a chemical-by-chemical approach.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers who sell organophosphates and farmers who rely on them would lose a pest-control tool, and compliance could add costs that may be passed into food prices.

drawbacks.text: A blanket ban on the whole organophosphate class removes pest-control options for growers regardless of residue level, which could raise farming costs and, potentially, food prices.

Because the EPA already banned chlorpyrifos from food in 2022, the bill's practical effect goes beyond the worst-known chemical and would prohibit other organophosphates even where the agency had set allowable tolerance levels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health rationale is straightforward: organophosphates are neurotoxic, and small residues on food are a particular concern for children's brain development. The trade-off is that a class-wide ban is blunt and would cost growers and pesticide makers a tool the current tolerance system permits. The bill got no hearing or vote, so the merits were never weighed in public by a committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in September 2023 and never advanced; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on September 18, 2023, with Reps. Bowman, Meng, Schakowsky, and Barragan as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on September 18, 2023, and to the Subcommittee on Health on September 22, 2023, where the trail ends.
The bill picked up 5 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action was taken through the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organophosphate pesticide makers and growers who use them, who keep selling and spraying a class of chemicals that would have been banned from food; consumers get no new protection beyond what existing EPA rules already provide.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide makers and growers still using organophosphates

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban organophosphate pesticides from food.

for.name: Jamaal Bowman, Grace Meng, Jan Schakowsky, Nanette Barragan
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a subcommittee or full-committee action; it sat at referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat, but because the bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote, no recorded position from Republicans or from the committee majority exists.

industries.note: The bill would outlaw their products from food outright, eliminating a class of sales. Consumers would gain the protection; the industry would lose revenue. Because the bill died, the industry kept the status quo.

industries.industry: Farmers and growers who use organophosphates
industries.note: Growers would lose a cheap, widely used insect-control tool and would need alternatives, which could raise their costs and food prices; at the same time farmworkers and rural residents near sprayed fields face the heaviest exposure to these neurotoxic chemicals. With the bill dead, they keep the tool and the exposure continues.
